title: The Development of Research Stations in Antarctica

paragraphs.text: Not many people get to work on the icy continent of Antarctica, and for many of those that do, it can prove a life-changing experience. Every year 2000 people including scientists, nurses, mechanics, artists and explorers travel south to Antarctica to work. They come from over 30 countries and, while some stay only a few days, others stay for a month or even a year or two. They may spend their time at the 40 permanent research stations scattered around the continent that are open year-round, or they may make use of the 30 stations that are used in the summer only.

The first buildings in Antarctica were the huts put up by explorers like Scott and Shackleton in the early 1900s. These simple wooden structures provided little more than basic shelter from the cold and wind. But today’s stations, such as Tor, which is home to only four people, to McMurdo Station, where over 1000 live at peak times, are much more sophisticated. Each station needs facilities for power generation and for dealing with waste, for making fresh water – either by melting snow or removing the salt from seawater – and for medical care. The stations must be able to store and prepare food, service vehicles, run telecommunications units and maintain laboratories.

Geology, surveying, meteorology and some biology were being undertaken in Antarctica by the UK, Chile and Argentina from the late 1940s. When the French built a station at Port Martin in 1950, they had hardly started their research before the station burnt down. The forerunner of many later science stations was Mawson, built by the Australians in 1954. Mawson Station led the first wave of building that occurred in response to the International Geophysical Year, which included McMurdo Station and then the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station in 1956. By 1958, 12 countries had constructed stations around Antarctica. One constant problem was drifting snow, which gradually buried the buildings. For this reason, windy, rocky places were usually the first choice of site, as they posed fewer problems than building on snow or ice.

Many of the modern research stations have been built since the late 1980s. Construction in Antarctica needs to be adapted to the harsh environment – this is definitely a challenging place to build. For example, structures that are built on top of snow or ice produce heat and can slowly sink if not well-insulated. In addition, drifting and blowing snow can damage buildings, and not only must pipes be protected from freezing temperatures, but wind with gusts over 270 kph not uncommon, windows in particular are at risk of being blown in, filling buildings with snow.

There is currently enthusiasm for rebuilding stations using modern engineering in order to solve some of these problems. For example, Neumayer Station has now been replaced by a two-storey structure that cannot be buried by snow. Called Neumayer III, it has been constructed with adjustable legs that can be lifted up as snow accumulates around it. The British Antarctic Survey has also built an advanced new station, which it opened in 2012. The Halley VI Station can be towed behind tractors as the weather changes, because the buildings have been fabricated on top of skis. This futuristic station has little in common with the early research facilities built in the 1950s.

These days, a great deal more consideration is given to the comfort of the human beings who will live and work in the stations, often for prolonged periods. At Halley VI, for example, as well as a comfortable accommodation block there is an extensive scientific laboratory. Then one of the modules has been designed specifically for socializing, and even has a pool where scientists can relax after work. At the smaller stations, scientists and support personnel typically share the responsibilities for meal preparation, but most of the larger facilities have a professional chef. It takes a lot of energy to fuel bodies working outside in extreme cold, so a nutritionist usually develops the menus.

There have been other significant developments as well. Fifty years ago, little concern was paid to the long-term environmental implications of human presence on the continent. Thankfully, a lot has changed. In 1991, the Protocol on Environmental Protection was added to the Antarctic Treaty. Since then, the focus of designing stations has shifted to one which has minimum impact on the environment, especially the penguins inhabiting numerous sites around the Antarctic coastline. Another innovation has been at South Pole station. It is forbidden to bring soil into Antarctica, so greenhouses cannot be used. But using a slowly circulating nutrient solution – called hydroponics – South Pole has successfully grown vegetables. It’s just one more example of how life has been transformed in Antarctica since the first explorers and scientists set up their stations on the continent.
